title: 15 places in New Jersey to take the grandkids
dek: Zoos, aquariums, farms and a battleship, chosen for children and grandparents alike. Here is where the benches, elevators and wheelchair rentals are, and what seniors pay.
keyFacts: Cape May County Park & Zoo charges nothing for admission or car parking.
Duke Farms and Howell Living History Farm are free. The New Jersey State Museum is free, with $10 planetarium shows.
Bergen County Zoo charges seniors 62+ just $2 (county residents) or $4.
Adventure Aquarium rents manual wheelchairs for $8 and scooters for $30, plus refundable deposits.
Space Farms Zoo & Museum's 2026 season ended November 1. It reopens in spring.
body:
A day out with the grandkids works best when it works for everyone. Little legs need a playground and a snack. Older knees need a bench, a level path and a restroom that is not a half mile away. New Jersey has plenty of places that manage both.

We checked the places below on their official websites in October 2026. We list prices only where the site posts them, and we say so when it does not. Hours shift a lot between fall and winter, and some spots close for the season, so call before you load the car.

Plan the day around the slowest walker and the youngest napper, and everyone has a better time.

How do I plan a day that works for both of us?

  1. Pick one main stop. Two attractions in one day sounds fun and usually ends in tears, some of them yours. Leave time for lunch and a sit-down.
  2. Look up the map before you go. Find the restrooms, the café, the elevators and the closest parking to the entrance. Many sites post an accessibility page.
  3. Ask about wheelchairs and strollers. Several places below lend or rent them, usually first come, first served. A rented wheelchair can turn a two-hour visit into a four-hour one.
  4. Go early on a weekday if you can. School-day mornings are quieter for toddlers and preschoolers, and parking is easier.
  5. Pack for two generations. Bring your medications, water, snacks, a change of clothes for the child and a charged phone. Write your cell number on a card in the child's pocket.
  6. Ask about senior rates. Many places discount for 62+ or 65+. Bring ID.

North Jersey: where should we go?

1. Turtle Back Zoo, West Orange

Essex County's zoo is compact and busy, with a train, a carousel and a touch tank. The zoo says plainly that it is built on a mountain and has steep paths, with benches throughout for breaks. A limited number of manual wheelchairs and strollers can be rented at Guest Relations, first come, first served, and the train is wheelchair accessible. Stroller rentals close for winter. Regular tickets were $22 for adults and $19 for seniors 62 and older and children 2 to 12 when we checked, and the zoo train is free to ride. Call 973-731-5800 ext. 0 for current rates.

2. Bergen County Zoo, Paramus

This small zoo inside Van Saun County Park is easy to cover in a morning, which makes it a good first zoo. Standard hours are 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., last entry at 4. Bergen County residents 62 and older pay $2 and out-of-county seniors pay $4. Children 3 to 14 pay $4 (residents) or $7, and children under 3 are free. The train and carousel cost $3 per person, per ride, sold only at the zoo booth. Questions: 201-634-3100.

3. Liberty Science Center, Jersey City

Four floors of hands-on science, plus a planetarium, all indoors. That makes it a strong pick for a cold or rainy day. Each floor has two large elevators, and a third serves the planetarium. Wheelchairs can be requested at the Welcome Desk. There is a drop-off area near the entrance for guests with special needs, reached from Phillip Street. Parking costs $7 for cars. The center is closed some weekdays, so check the schedule. Prices are posted only through the online ticket system, and buying a day ahead gets the best price. Call 201-200-1000.

4. Paterson Great Falls, Paterson

Kids love the roar. The Passaic River drops about 77 feet between dark cliffs, and the view from the overlook railing is free. It is a short visit, which suits a child with a short attention span. Overlook Park has accessible parking, but paths mix paved and unpaved sections. There are no restrooms in the park. Accessible restrooms are at the Paterson Museum, 2 Market Street. Park office: 973-523-0370.

5. Silas Condict County Park, Kinnelon

A quiet nature outing for grandkids who like to throw sticks in water and look for ducks. The park covers 1,513 acres with more than 10 miles of trails. The easy part is the seven-acre lake, which has benches and is partly lined with weeping cherry trees. There are picnic sites with tables and grills. It is open sunrise to sunset. The county page does not describe accessibility, so call 973-326-7600 before bringing a wheelchair.

6. Space Farms Zoo & Museum, Wantage

Part zoo, part old-time museum. More than 500 animals share the grounds with nine museum buildings holding over 50 antique cars, carriages, dolls and farm machines. Grandparents often enjoy the museum as much as the kids enjoy the bears. There is a picnic area, a playground and a pizza restaurant. The 2026 season ended Sunday, November 1, so plan this one for spring. In season, hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., last entrance 4 p.m. Daily tickets start at $26. The site does not post a senior rate or accessibility details. Call 973-875-3223.

Central Jersey: what is worth the drive?

7. Duke Farms, Hillsborough

Doris Duke's former estate is now 2,700 acres of meadows, woods and ponds, and entry is always free. More than 15 miles of trails are mostly flat, paved and wider than 36 inches, which is great for strollers and wheelchairs. The Orchid Range is a walk from the Farm Barn, so Duke Farms offers a free round-trip accessibility transport there for people with limited mobility, by reservation. There are benches along the path to the Farm Barn. The campus is closed every Sunday and Monday. Saturdays in the busy season need a free parking pass.

8. Grounds For Sculpture, Hamilton

Giant outdoor sculptures hide around every bend, which turns a walk into a treasure hunt. The main path is paved, though side paths can be gravel, sand or steep. Wheelchairs rent for $15 a day and scooters for $29 for the first four hours. Seniors 65 and older pay $18 (adults $25). Timed tickets must be booked online in advance. Closed Tuesdays from September through May.

9. New Jersey State Museum and Planetarium, Trenton

Dinosaurs, fossils and Native American history, next to the State House. General admission is free. Planetarium shows cost $10, with $1 off for seniors 65 and older. Use the Planetarium entrance if walking is hard. Every level has two elevators, most galleries have benches, and the front desk lends one free wheelchair. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

10. Howell Living History Farm, Hopewell Township

A working farm run as it was around 1900, with horses, plowing and real chores. Kids can often lend a hand. Admission and parking are free (the corn maze has a fee). It is open Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and closed Sundays, Mondays and Mercer County holidays. The Visitor Center is fully accessible, and transportation to the barnyard and fields is available on request. Picnicking is not allowed, so plan lunch elsewhere. Call 609-737-3299.

11. Jenkinson's Aquarium, Point Pleasant Beach

A manageable, indoor aquarium right on the boardwalk, with penguins, seals and sharks. Seniors 65 and older pay $15, adults $19 and children 3 to 11 pay $13. Children 2 and under are free. Fall and winter hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily, closed Thanksgiving and Christmas. The wheelchair lift is being replaced and is out of service until about November 30, so call 732-892-0600 if anyone in your group needs it.

South Jersey: where can we spend a whole day?

12. Adventure Aquarium, Camden

Big and dramatic, with a shark bridge, hippos and penguins. The average visit runs two to three hours. General admission starts at $32.99 for adults and $27.99 for children, and seniors save $2. Manual wheelchairs rent for $8 (plus a $10 refundable deposit) and electric scooters for $30 (plus $50). Single strollers rent for $8. You may bring outside food. Parking is $10. The aquarium is mostly cashless. It is open 364 days a year, closed Thanksgiving. Call 1-844-474-3474.

13. Battleship New Jersey, Camden

A real Iowa-class battleship, docked across from Philadelphia. School-age kids tend to love it. It is full of steep ladders, but wheelchair users can reach the main deck exterior and the officers' wardroom using elevators, and there is a main deck tour of about 45 minutes that skips the ladders. A senior rate is not posted, so ask. To arrange accessible parking, call 1-866-877-6262 ext. 108.

14. Storybook Land, Egg Harbor Township

A gentle amusement park built around nursery rhymes, sized for small children. Seniors pay $39.95 online or at the door. Other visitors 2 to 64 pay $42.95 online or $45.95 at the gate, and children under 2 are free. Its ticketed Christmas Fantasy with Lights season begins November 14, 2026, open 2 p.m. to 9 p.m., and runs through December. Holiday tickets may be priced differently, so check the website for dates and prices. An Assisted Access Pass at Guest Services helps guests who struggle with lines. Call 609-646-0103.

15. Cape May County Park & Zoo, Cape May Court House

One of the best deals in the state. Admission and car parking are free, and the zoo is open every day except Christmas. Zoo hours are 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. in summer and 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. in winter. Strollers, wheelchairs and motorized scooters are available to rent. Two playgrounds sit just outside the zoo entrance. Outside food is allowed in the park but not inside the zoo, so plan a picnic before or after.

What are the common mistakes?

  • Trying to see everything. Pick the three animals or exhibits the child cares about most. Anything else is a bonus.
  • Skipping the rental. If you get tired after an hour of walking, rent the wheelchair or scooter. The child can ride along for a stretch, and you will both last longer.
  • Forgetting seasonal closures. Space Farms is closed from November until spring, Duke Farms is closed Sundays and Mondays, and Grounds For Sculpture is closed Tuesdays from September through May.
  • Not bringing paperwork. If a parent is not along, carry a signed note with their phone number, the child's allergies and the pediatrician's name.

For more places to go, see our guides to day trips and free and discounted outings. If you are 62 or older, the free NJ Senior Citizen Pass also gets you into state parks without paying the entrance fee.

faq.q: Which of these places are free?
faq.a: Cape May County Park & Zoo, Duke Farms, Howell Living History Farm, the New Jersey State Museum (planetarium shows are extra) and the Paterson Great Falls overlook charge no admission. Silas Condict County Park is also free to visit.

faq.q: Where can I rent a wheelchair or scooter?
faq.a: Adventure Aquarium, Grounds For Sculpture and Cape May County Park & Zoo rent them. Turtle Back Zoo has a limited number for rent, and Liberty Science Center and the New Jersey State Museum have wheelchairs at the front desk. Supplies are small, so arrive early or call ahead.

faq.q: What is a good indoor choice for a cold or rainy day?
faq.a: Liberty Science Center, Adventure Aquarium, Jenkinson's Aquarium and the New Jersey State Museum are mostly or fully indoors. Check hours first, since Liberty Science Center closes on some weekdays.

faq.q: Do I need a note from the parents to take my grandchild out?
faq.a: It is smart to carry one. A signed note with the parents' phone numbers, the child's allergies and the pediatrician's name helps if there is an emergency or a medical visit.

faq.q: Which New Jersey zoos give seniors a discount?
faq.a: Bergen County Zoo charges seniors 62 and older $2 if they live in Bergen County and $4 if not. Turtle Back Zoo had a $19 senior ticket for ages 62 and older when we checked, and Cape May County Park & Zoo is free for everyone.

faq.q: Can I bring a picnic lunch?
faq.a: It depends on the place. Adventure Aquarium allows outside food, and Cape May County Park allows it in the park but not inside the zoo. Howell Living History Farm does not allow picnicking, so plan lunch elsewhere.

title: How to stay active and social through a New Jersey winter
dek: Indoor walking spots, the gym benefit hiding in your Medicare plan, warming centers and the real risks of shoveling. A practical plan for the cold months.
keyFacts: Cherry Hill Mall opens at 9 a.m. daily for walkers. Bridgewater Commons walkers can start at 6:30 a.m. Monday to Saturday.
SilverSneakers and Renew Active come with many Medicare Advantage plans at no extra cost. Original Medicare does not cover gyms.
A Code Blue is declared at 32 degrees or below, or a wind chill of zero or below for two hours. Check nj211.org/njcodeblue.
The Winter Termination Program protects eligible households from utility shutoffs November 15 to March 15.
Driving with snow on your car can cost $25 to $75, or $200 to $1,000 if it causes injury or damage.
body:
A New Jersey winter can shrink your world fast. A week of ice, an early sunset and a car that stays in the driveway can leave you inside more than is good for body or mood. The fix is a plan made now, while the roads are still clear.

This guide covers where to walk indoors, how to use the fitness benefit that may already come with your Medicare plan, where to find company on gray afternoons, and how to stay safe when the cold turns serious. We checked every detail against official sources in October 2026.

The best time to plan for February is a sunny afternoon in October.

Where can I walk indoors when it is icy?

Malls have long doubled as winter walking tracks. They are flat, heated and lit, and there are benches and restrooms every few hundred feet. Several New Jersey malls officially welcome walkers before stores open:

  • Cherry Hill Mall opens early every morning for mall walkers. Doors open at 9 a.m., seven days a week.
  • Moorestown Mall welcomes walkers one hour before posted shopping hours each day.
  • Bridgewater Commons hosts HealthHike, a free walking program run with RWJ University Hospital Somerset. Walkers can start as early as 6:30 a.m. Monday through Saturday and at 9 a.m. Sunday. Sign up at the mall management office on weekdays to get an ID badge and a mileage card. Monthly meetings with health speakers run October through June. Call 908-595-2345.

Mall hours change, so confirm on the mall's website before you go. If no mall near you has a program, ask your town's recreation department or senior center. Some community centers and schools open gyms or tracks to residents in winter. Your local YMCA is another option, and many Ys take the Medicare fitness benefits described below.

Does my Medicare plan pay for a gym?

Original Medicare does not cover gym memberships. Many Medicare Advantage plans, and some Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans, include a fitness program at no extra cost. The two you will hear about most are SilverSneakers and Renew Active.

SilverSneakers

SilverSneakers is offered through select Medicare Advantage and Medicare Supplement plans. Your eligibility depends on your plan, not your income. Here is how it works:

  1. Check eligibility. Use the SilverSneakers eligibility checker with the name and member ID exactly as they appear on your insurance card.
  2. Get your member ID. Create an account at SilverSneakers.com and download or print your SilverSneakers ID.
  3. Pick a location. Use the location finder to see partner gyms near you.
  4. Show your ID at the front desk. That is it. Classes held at community centers and parks, plus live and on-demand online classes, are included too.

Renew Active

Renew Active comes only with UnitedHealthcare Medicare plans. It includes a standard gym membership at participating locations at no additional cost, plus online classes and brain-health content. The gym network varies by plan and area, and not every plan includes it. Questions: 1-855-604-1588 (TTY 711).

Shopping for a plan right now?

Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. If a fitness benefit matters to you, check each plan's Evidence of Coverage before you switch. For free, unbiased help comparing plans, call New Jersey's SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820. Our guide to Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap explains the trade-offs.

Where can I find company on long winter days?

Your public library is often the warmest, friendliest building in town. Most New Jersey libraries run free book clubs, movie afternoons, technology help, craft groups and lectures through the winter. Many county library systems post their calendars online, and staff will gladly read the schedule to you over the phone.

Senior centers are the other anchor. Expect exercise classes, cards, lunch programs and day trips. Some arrange rides for members. To find the center nearest you, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 or dial 2-1-1.

Holiday light shows and seasonal events help break up December. Parks, zoos and botanical gardens around the state run evening light displays, and many towns hold tree lightings and holiday markets. Storybook Land in Egg Harbor Township, for example, runs a ticketed Christmas season with lights from November 14 through December. Check each event's website for dates, as schedules are often set late in the fall. Weeknights tend to be less crowded, and some displays can be seen from a car.

What is a Code Blue, and where can I go to get warm?

Under New Jersey law, a county declares a Code Blue when temperatures will reach 32 degrees Fahrenheit or lower, or when the National Weather Service wind chill will be zero or below for at least two hours. During a Code Blue, counties open warming centers. These are mainly for people without shelter, but anyone who loses heat at home can ask for help.

  • Check current activations and warming centers by county at nj211.org/njcodeblue.
  • Call 2-1-1 or the Statewide Homeless Hotline at 1-877-652-1148 after hours.
  • Many public libraries, shopping centers and senior centers serve as warming spots during business hours.

Staying safe in the cold

Aging makes it harder to notice when your body is getting too cold. The National Institute on Aging advises setting your heat to at least 68 degrees, since even a home at 60 to 65 degrees can lead to hypothermia in older adults. Wear layers indoors, close the curtains at night and limit alcohol.

Know the warning signs of hypothermia: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness. Hypothermia is a medical emergency. Call 9-1-1.

Behind on the heating bill?

New Jersey's Winter Termination Program protects eligible households from utility shutoffs from November 15 through March 15. You may qualify if you receive PAAD, Lifeline, the Universal Service Fund, home energy assistance (LIHEAP) or SSI, or if you cannot pay because of illness, medical bills, job loss or a death in the family. LIHEAP applications are open October 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. See our guide to food and utility help.

What should I do now to get ready?

A few calls this fall can save a lot of trouble in January. Work through this list before Thanksgiving.

  1. Check your heat. Have the furnace or boiler serviced, test your carbon monoxide and smoke alarms, and set the thermostat to at least 68 degrees.
  2. Apply for heating help early. LIHEAP and Universal Service Fund applications opened October 1, 2026, and run to June 30, 2027. Approval also helps you qualify for the Winter Termination Program.
  3. Review your Medicare plan. Open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. If you want SilverSneakers or Renew Active, confirm the plan you pick includes it.
  4. Line up snow help. Ask a neighbor, a relative or a local volunteer group now, before the first storm.
  5. Stock up. Keep a week of medications, easy food, flashlights, batteries and a phone charger at home, and a winter kit in the car.
  6. Save the numbers. Write down 2-1-1, your utility, your doctor and a neighbor, and keep the list by the phone.

Should I still shovel snow?

Think hard before you pick up the shovel. The American Heart Association warns that shoveling heavy snow can raise the risk of a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest. It is mostly arm work, which strains the heart more than leg work. People often hold their breath while lifting, and cold air tightens blood vessels.

The AHA's advice is direct. If you have heart disease or risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking or a past heart attack or stroke, have someone else clear the snow. If you must do it yourself:

  • Start slowly and take breaks.
  • Push or sweep snow rather than lifting and throwing it. Use a snow blower if you have one.
  • Cover your nose and mouth and dress in layers, with a hat and gloves.
  • Stop right away if you feel chest pain or pressure, lightheadedness or a racing or irregular heartbeat. Call 9-1-1 if it does not ease quickly.

Line up help before the first storm. A neighbor's teenager, a local landscaper or a church volunteer group can be booked in advance. Keep a bag of ice melt or sand by the door, and wear rubber-soled, low-heeled boots.

How do I handle winter driving, or not driving at all?

New Jersey law requires you to clear all snow and ice from your vehicle, including the hood, windows and roof, before you drive. Fines run $25 to $75 per offense, even if nothing flies off. If flying ice or snow causes injury or property damage, fines rise to $200 to $1,000.

The state's winter driving advice:

  • Drive at or below the speed limit and leave 8 to 10 seconds behind the car ahead.
  • Give snowplows plenty of room and avoid passing them.
  • If you skid, take your foot off the gas and gently steer in the direction the rear of the car is sliding.
  • Keep a kit in the car: ice scraper, blanket, flashlight, phone charger, water and snacks.
  • Check road conditions at 511nj.org before you leave.

Winter is also a natural time to think about cutting back. Many people stop driving at night or in bad weather first. Our guide to driving later in life covers how to make that call and what transportation options exist. NJ Transit offers reduced fares for riders 62 and older, and county transportation services can help with medical trips and errands.

When you cannot get out, keep in touch on purpose. Set up a daily check-in call with a friend or relative, join a phone or video group through your library or senior center, and arrange grocery and prescription delivery before a storm hits. See our guide to staying connected for more ideas.

faq.q: Does Original Medicare pay for SilverSneakers?
faq.a: No. SilverSneakers comes through select Medicare Advantage and Medicare Supplement plans. Renew Active comes only with UnitedHealthcare Medicare plans. Check your plan's Evidence of Coverage or call SHIP at 1-800-792-8820 for help comparing plans.

faq.q: How do I find a warming center near me?
faq.a: Visit nj211.org/njcodeblue to see which counties have a Code Blue in effect and where warming centers are open. You can also dial 2-1-1 or call 1-877-652-1148. Libraries and senior centers often serve as warm places during business hours.

faq.q: What temperature should I keep my home in winter?
faq.a: The National Institute on Aging recommends at least 68 degrees. Even a home kept at 60 to 65 degrees can lead to hypothermia in older adults.

faq.q: Is it safe for me to shovel snow?
faq.a: The American Heart Association advises people with heart disease or risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes or a past heart attack to have someone else do it. If you shovel, go slowly, push rather than lift, and stop if you feel chest pain or lightheaded.

faq.q: Can my utility shut off my heat in winter?
faq.a: If you qualify for the Winter Termination Program, your service cannot be cut off from November 15 through March 15. Recipients of PAAD, Lifeline, USF, LIHEAP and SSI qualify, as do people facing hardship such as illness or job loss. Contact your utility to enroll.

faq.q: What is a Code Blue in New Jersey?
faq.a: A county declares a Code Blue when temperatures will reach 32 degrees or lower, or when the wind chill will be zero or below for at least two hours. Counties then open warming centers, and current activations are listed at nj211.org/njcodeblue.

title: Mahjong, canasta and bridge for seniors in New Jersey
dek: Why table games are good company for the mind, how long each one takes to learn, where to find lessons and games in New Jersey, and how to keep playing at home, including with someone who has memory loss.
keyFacts: Group courses in North Jersey usually run 3 to 4 weekly sessions of about 2 hours, often about $200 a person (our October 2026 conversations).
American mahjong uses a new National Mah Jongg League card every year. The 2026 card costs $14, or $15 in large print.
The American Contract Bridge League offers a free 75-minute Zoom intro class and a free guest membership.
The National Institute on Aging links strong social ties to better thinking skills, but says proof that hobbies prevent decline is not definitive.
Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to find game afternoons at a senior center near you.
body:
Walk into almost any New Jersey senior center on a weekday afternoon and you will hear it: the click of mahjong tiles, a shuffle of cards, someone laughing about a hand that went wrong. Mahjong, canasta and bridge have kept friendships going for generations. They give the week a shape, and they give people a reason to get dressed and go out.

This guide is for older adults who want to learn or return to these games, and for sons, daughters and spouses who are looking for something their mom or dad will actually look forward to. It covers what the research says, how hard each game is, how lessons usually work, where to play in New Jersey and how to keep a game going at home.

Are card and tile games good for the brain?

The honest answer is that they are good for people, and probably good for the brain, but nobody can promise they prevent memory loss.

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says staying engaged in meaningful activities may have cognitive benefits. It points to one study where older adults who learned demanding new skills, quilting or digital photography, had more memory improvement than people who only socialized. It also notes that evidence for a lasting effect from these kinds of activities is not definitive, and it warns readers to be wary of claims that computer brain games can improve memory and thinking.

The social side has stronger support. NIA reports that in its long running Health and Retirement Study, people 65 and older with high social engagement had better cognitive health later in life. Its list of ways to stay connected starts with a simple one: play cards or other games with friends, in person or online.

That is where these games shine. You have to remember what has been played, plan a few moves ahead and read your partners. You also have to show up, every week, with the same people. In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, families and care professionals, the outcomes people named again and again were staying sharp, seeing people and having something to look forward to every week.

The best brain game is the one that gets you out of the house every Tuesday.

How hard is each game to learn?

Mahjong

Most groups in New Jersey play American mahjong, which uses tiles and a printed card of winning hands. The National Mah Jongg League (NMJL) publishes a new card every year, so even longtime players relearn some hands every year. The 2026 card costs $14 in standard size and $15 in large print, which is easier on the eyes. The League also sells an online version of the game by subscription for people who want to practice from home.

Instructors told us you cannot really learn mahjong in one lesson. Four weeks works better than three. They also said the game has become very popular with younger players, often people in their late 30s to mid 50s. Some newcomers over 65 found the first lessons overwhelming. People who already play, though, often keep playing well into their 80s.

Canasta

Canasta is a rummy style card game where you build sets of matching cards. Many people find it gentler to learn than mahjong or bridge, and it is easy to play at a kitchen table. Instructors told us it is harder to teach online than mahjong, so in person lessons are best.

Bridge

Bridge is the most demanding of the three. Instructors described it as the hardest to learn and the most mentally taxing. It is played by four people in two partnerships, with a bidding stage before any cards are played. That challenge is part of the appeal. People who love bridge tend to love it for life.

How are lessons usually taught?

Most teachers in North Jersey teach in small groups. In our October 2026 conversations, mahjong, canasta and bridge instructors described a typical course like this:

  • Group size: about 3 to 8 students at one table.
  • Length: 3 to 4 weekly sessions, each about 2 hours.
  • Cost: often about $200 per person for the whole course.
  • Format: some teach mahjong over Zoom. Canasta and bridge usually work better face to face.

Private lessons at home cost more. Instructors we spoke with generally charge about $60 to $150 an hour for one on one teaching at home, depending on the activity and how far they travel. A home lesson makes the most sense when getting out is hard, or when a group of friends wants to learn together around their own table.

Senior center and library classes are often free or low cost, so ask there first. Prices change, so confirm with whoever runs the class.

Where can I learn or play in New Jersey?

Senior centers. Many New Jersey senior centers host weekly mahjong, canasta or bridge games, and some offer beginner lessons. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 connects you to your county office on aging, which can tell you what centers near you offer. You can also browse our county pages, including our guide to senior centers in Essex County.

Public libraries. Many libraries run open mahjong or card afternoons, and some offer beginner series. Check your library's events calendar or ask at the desk.

JCCs, community colleges and lifelong learning programs. Jewish community centers in New Jersey often have strong mahjong and bridge groups open to the whole community. Community college continuing education departments and lifelong learning programs sometimes offer game classes too. Our guide to learning something new lists programs for older adults around the state.

Bridge clubs. The American Contract Bridge League (ACBL) is the governing body for bridge in North America. Its website has a club directory you can search by city, state or ZIP code, plus directories of classes and teachers. Two ACBL units serve North and Central Jersey: the North Jersey Bridge Association (Unit 106) and the New Jersey Bridge League (Unit 140), both part of ACBL District 3. Southern New Jersey falls in District 4, where the Philadelphia Contract Bridge Association (Unit 141) lists clubs including the South Jersey Bridge Club.

For complete beginners, the ACBL runs Trickstarter, a free 75-minute Zoom class that teaches a simplified version of the game with no bidding. It also offers a free guest membership with games just for newer players. The ACBL help desk is at 662-253-3191.

Getting there

Many older adults stop playing only because they can no longer drive to the game. If that is the issue, ask your county office on aging about senior transportation, look at our guide to driving later in life, or move the game to your living room.

How do I start a regular game at home?

A home game is one of the easiest ways to keep someone social, especially after surgery, a move or giving up the car.

  1. Find your table. Bridge needs four players, and mahjong is usually played with four. Canasta is more flexible. Ask neighbors, old friends, people from your house of worship or a senior center group.
  2. Pick a standing time. Same day, same hour, every week. A routine makes it more likely people come back.
  3. Set up for comfort. Good lighting, a sturdy table and chairs with arms. Large print cards, a large print mahjong card and card holders help with arthritis and low vision.
  4. Keep the stakes small. Many groups play for nickels or for nothing. The point is the company.
  5. Bring in a teacher if needed. A few home lessons can get a new group started. If a stranger is coming into the home, read our guide to vetting in-home help first.

If your parent lives far away, a weekly video call game can work too. Many families pair this with help from a grandchild who sets up the tablet. Our guide to getting tech help can make that easier.

Can someone with memory loss still play?

Often, yes, at least for a while, and with some changes. Long practiced skills can last longer than new memories. A person who played bridge for 50 years may still recognize a good hand even when other things are slipping.

The National Institute on Aging suggests matching the activity to what the person can do now, helping them get started, watching for frustration and making sure they feel successful. It also says it is fine for someone to simply watch if they enjoy that more.

  • Simplify the game. Play open hands, skip the bidding or play a simpler cousin of the game, like rummy or a matching game with the mahjong tiles.
  • Play as partners. Sit beside them and make decisions together so they stay in the game.
  • Keep it short. Thirty to forty five minutes may be plenty. Stop while it is still fun.
  • Choose the best time of day. Many people with dementia do better in the morning or early afternoon.
  • Stay kind about mistakes. Nobody needs to be corrected on the rules. The goal is connection.

A care manager we spoke with described a client with dementia who had stopped going to his bridge club and would welcome a partner to play with him at home. If the club no longer works, a patient friend, family member or paid companion can keep the game alive at the kitchen table.

For more ideas, see our guides to activities for dementia and staying connected.

faq.q: Is it too late to learn mahjong or bridge at 75?
faq.a: No. Plenty of people learn in their 70s and beyond. Choose a beginner group, plan on at least four lessons, and practice between classes. Bridge takes the longest to learn, so canasta or mahjong may be an easier start.

faq.q: How much do mahjong or bridge lessons cost in New Jersey?
faq.a: In our October 2026 conversations with North Jersey instructors, a group course of 3 to 4 weekly sessions was often about $200 a person. Private lessons at home generally ran about $60 to $150 an hour. Senior center and library classes are often free or low cost.

faq.q: My mom used to play bridge but stopped after her dementia diagnosis. How can we get her playing again?
faq.a: Try a relaxed game at home with a patient partner who sits beside her. Simplify the rules, keep sessions short and play at her best time of day. If bridge is too much now, a simpler card game with the same friends can keep the social part going.

faq.q: Where do I buy the mahjong card?
faq.a: The National Mah Jongg League sells it on its website. The 2026 card is $14 for the standard size and $15 for large print. A new card comes out every year.

faq.q: How do I find a bridge club near me?
faq.a: Use the club directory on the American Contract Bridge League website and search by ZIP code. Many clubs offer games for newer players. You can also call the ACBL at 662-253-3191.

title: Theater matinees and senior tickets in NJ: a family guide
dek: Which New Jersey theaters offer senior discounts, when the matinees are, and how Paper Mill, State Theatre, NJPAC, McCarter, George Street and Two River help with hearing, wheelchairs, parking and trains.
keyFacts: Two River Theater in Red Bank gives patrons 65 and older 10% off each ticket with valid ID.
Paper Mill Playhouse matinees are Thursday, Saturday and Sunday at 1:30 p.m.
Every theater in this guide offers assistive listening; McCarter and George Street lend devices free.
State Theatre New Jersey sets aside $10 tickets for Medicaid card holders at every State Theatre presented show.
Paper Mill is renovating its lobby through summer 2027. The mezzanine is closed, but all accessible seating remains.
body:
Most of New Jersey's big professional theaters run afternoon matinees, which suit older adults who would rather not drive home in the dark. True senior discounts are less common than people expect. Two River Theater in Red Bank gives 10 percent off to patrons 65 and older. Paper Mill Playhouse, State Theatre New Jersey, McCarter and George Street focus instead on group rates, access discounts and other offers.

Every theater in this guide offers assistive listening and wheelchair seating. Below is what each one publishes on its own website about matinees, prices, hearing help, parking and getting there, so you can plan an afternoon out with your mom or dad.

Do New Jersey theaters offer senior discounts?

A few do, most do not. Of the theaters in this guide, only Two River lists a standing senior discount on its own site. The others offer group, access and multi-show savings instead.

TheaterWhat it publishes
Two River, Red Bank10% off at 65+ with ID; some $25 seats each show
Paper Mill, MillburnNo senior rate; groups of 10+ up to 25% off
State Theatre, New BrunswickNo senior rate; 2 shows save 10%, 3+ up to 20%
NJPAC, NewarkNo senior rate; 3+ shows save 15%
George Street, New BrunswickMost shows from $28 plus $7 fee
McCarter, Princeton$40 seats at captioned, described and ASL shows

Medicaid card holders should know about two programs. State Theatre New Jersey sets aside $10 tickets for every State Theatre presented performance for people enrolled in NJ's Families First Discovery Program and for Medicaid card holders. Paper Mill also takes part in the Families First Discovery Pass for people enrolled in state assistance programs. Patrons who use access services at Paper Mill, such as wheelchair seating or captioning, pay the lowest standard rate. If your parent is on NJ FamilyCare, ask the box office about it.

For more ways to stretch a fixed income, see our guide to free and discounted things to do after 60.

When are the matinees?

Paper Mill Playhouse runs matinees Thursday, Saturday and Sunday at 1:30 p.m. McCarter and George Street hold their captioned and described shows on weekend afternoons, mostly at 2 p.m. Times vary by production, so check each calendar.

  • Paper Mill Playhouse. Evenings Wednesday to Saturday at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday at 7 p.m. Matinees Thursday, Saturday and Sunday at 1:30 p.m. Box office: 973-376-4343.
  • McCarter Theatre. Its access performances for the 2026 to 2027 season are listed as Saturday and Sunday afternoons, mostly at 2 p.m. A Christmas Carol has 1 p.m. performances on December 19 and 20. Patron services: 609-258-2787.
  • George Street Playhouse. Captioned and audio-described shows are scheduled as 2 p.m. matinees, such as 2 Pianos, 4 Hands on December 12. Patron Services: 732-246-7717.
  • Two River Theater. Box office: 732-345-1400, noon to 6 p.m. Monday to Saturday.
  • State Theatre New Jersey. Ticket hotline: 732-246-7469.

Buy from the theater's own box office or website. Paper Mill, State Theatre and NJPAC all warn that resale sites can charge inflated prices. Many theaters will hold tickets at will call, which helps if your parent does not use a smartphone.

Can my parent hear the show? Assistive listening and captions

Yes. Paper Mill, State Theatre, NJPAC, McCarter, George Street and Two River all offer assistive listening. Ask at the box office or patron services desk when you arrive.

  • McCarter lends assistive listening devices free at the access services window in the lower lobby. You leave a name and phone number. Neck loops are available for hearing aids with a T-coil.
  • George Street provides assistive listening free at every performance on request, plus a loop option for hearing aid users.
  • NJPAC has an FM system with under-the-chin headsets and neck loops for T-coil users. It asks for a driver's license or credit card as a deposit.
  • Two River offers wireless FM headsets at the box office and large print programs.
  • State Theatre has an FM and Wi-Fi listening system in the auditorium that also works through the WaveCAST app on a smartphone.
  • Paper Mill lends assistive listening devices, and says its standard access services continue during this season's construction.

Open-captioned performances put the dialogue on a screen beside the stage. They help anyone who misses words, not only people with a diagnosed hearing loss. If your parent has hearing aids, ask their audiologist whether the T-coil setting is turned on. Our guide to hearing aids for older adults explains more.

Open captions help anyone who keeps asking "What did she say?"

Is the theater easy to get into with a walker or wheelchair?

All of these theaters have wheelchair seating with companion seats. Book those seats when you buy tickets, not at the door. Steps to the balcony are the main thing to watch.

  • State Theatre New Jersey has wheelchair spaces and aisle transfer seats in the orchestra. Staff can help from the front door to your seat, and a courtesy wheelchair is available at the Concierge Desk. Most balcony seats require climbing steps.
  • McCarter offers 30-inch wide seats, with or without armrests, on request through Patron Services.
  • Two River has on-grade entrances, elevators and integrated wheelchair seating. You can ask for a wheelchair to get to your seat and have it stored if you transfer.
  • NJPAC reaches every level by elevator. Call ticket services at 973-297-5843 at least two weeks ahead with special requests.
  • George Street theaters and restrooms are wheelchair accessible, and an elevator in the lobby goes to the balcony.
Paper Mill during construction

Paper Mill is renovating its lobby, restaurant and outdoor spaces and is presenting four shows instead of five this season, with work scheduled to finish by the end of summer 2027. The auditorium is untouched and all accessible seating remains, but the mezzanine is closed. The accessible entrance is on the Brookside Drive side, so the theater suggests parking in Lots B, C or D. Lot D is not available during weekday matinees while school is in session. Portable restrooms are stationed near the entrances. Call 973-376-4343 with questions.

McCarter also offers relaxed performances, with house lights partly on and freedom to talk or step out. It specifically welcomes people with dementia. One is scheduled for A Christmas Carol on Saturday, December 26 at 3 p.m. For more ideas, see things to do with a parent who has dementia.

How do we get there without driving?

Several theaters sit near NJ Transit stations. Riders 62 and older can get reduced fares. See our guide to NJ Transit reduced fares.

  • Two River Theater is one block from the North Jersey Coast Line in Red Bank and has free on-site parking.
  • Paper Mill is a 5 to 10 minute walk from the Millburn train station. Its free shuttle runs from the train station commuter Lot 7 after 6 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends, starting two hours before the show. During construction it drops off in front of the building. On-site lots cost $12.
  • State Theatre New Jersey is a few blocks from the New Brunswick station on the Northeast Corridor. Show proof of NJ Transit ridership for 20% off select shows. The theater has no lot of its own. Valet is $20 for three hours from the Heldrich Hotel across the street, and a few accessible spots are out front on a first come basis.
  • NJPAC has parking in the Military Park Garage across the street, with accessible spaces next to the elevator on all three levels.

If your parent lives in an active adult community, the New Jersey Symphony runs coaches to its Thursday matinee concerts at NJPAC from a list of communities for $14 per concert, with reservations required at 1-800-255-3476. The Symphony also says discounted tickets are available for seniors, based on availability. If your parent has recently given up driving, our guide to when a parent stops driving covers rides and other options.

How do I plan lunch and a show for my mom?

Book a matinee, pick a restaurant within a short walk, and arrive early. Paper Mill suggests arriving at least an hour before curtain to park and pick up tickets. NJPAC opens its doors an hour before showtime.

  1. Choose the seats first. Aisle or orchestra seats save stairs. Ask the box office about wheelchair, transfer or wider seats.
  2. Book lunch close by. Paper Mill's restaurant is part of this season's renovation, so plan to eat in town first. Two River lists partner restaurants a few blocks away in Red Bank. Downtown New Brunswick has dozens of restaurants near State Theatre and George Street.
  3. Plan the restroom and break. Most shows have one intermission. Ask the run time when you buy so you can plan medication and meals.
  4. Know the exchange rules. Tickets are generally nonrefundable. Paper Mill allows exchanges to another performance of the same show for $5 a ticket, with a matinee deadline of 5 p.m. the previous business day. George Street needs 24 hours' notice and charges $10 a ticket for non-subscribers. McCarter charges $25 per order. Do not book a far-off date if health is unpredictable.
  5. Consider a group. Many senior centers organize theater trips. At Paper Mill, State Theatre and Two River, group rates start at 10 people. NJPAC also offers $6 tickets to nonprofit social service groups in and around Newark. Our county pages link to local senior centers.

Community theaters, high school musicals and college productions are often cheaper still, and many run Sunday matinees. Check your town's website or library. For the December season, our holiday events guide lists more ideas.

Prices change

Theaters change prices, discounts and schedules often, and some use demand-based pricing. Confirm the current offer with the box office before you buy.

faq.q: Which New Jersey theaters give senior discounts?
faq.a: Two River Theater in Red Bank gives patrons 65 and older 10% off each ticket with valid ID. Paper Mill, State Theatre New Jersey, NJPAC and McCarter do not list a standing senior discount, but offer group rates, multi-show savings and discounted access performances. Call the box office to ask about current offers.

faq.q: What time are Paper Mill Playhouse matinees?
faq.a: Paper Mill Playhouse runs matinees Thursday, Saturday and Sunday at 1:30 p.m. Evening shows are Wednesday to Saturday at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday at 7 p.m. The box office number is 973-376-4343.

faq.q: How do I get my mom a hearing device at the theater?
faq.a: Ask at the box office or patron services desk when you arrive. McCarter and George Street lend assistive listening devices free, and McCarter, NJPAC and George Street have options for hearing aids with a T-coil. NJPAC asks for a driver's license or credit card as a deposit.

faq.q: How do I take my dad, who uses a wheelchair, to a show in NJ?
faq.a: Reserve wheelchair and companion seats when you buy tickets, since they go first come, first served. State Theatre New Jersey and Two River can help you from the door to your seat, and NJPAC asks for special requests two weeks ahead at 973-297-5843. At Paper Mill this season, use the Brookside Drive accessible entrance.

faq.q: Can my parent get to a theater by train?
faq.a: Yes. Two River Theater is one block from the Red Bank station, Paper Mill is a 5 to 10 minute walk from Millburn station, and State Theatre New Jersey is a few blocks from the New Brunswick station. NJ Transit offers reduced fares to riders 62 and older.

title: Senior bus trips in NJ: how town and senior center trips work
dek: How New Jersey towns and senior centers run group day trips, what they cost, what to ask if your parent uses a walker, and how to check that a bus company is safe.
keyFacts: Most senior bus trips are run by town recreation departments, senior centers and senior clubs, each with its own age rule (often 55, 60 or 65).
Many town programs give no refunds once you pay, so check the policy first.
Interstate motorcoach companies must have a USDOT number and at least $5 million in insurance, according to FMCSA.
Popular trips fill up fast, so sign up as soon as the flyer comes out.
The toll-free aging and disability line, 1-877-222-3737, connects you to your county office on aging.
body:
Many New Jersey towns and senior centers run group bus trips for older adults. A typical trip leaves from a town building or shopping center parking lot in the morning, heads to a museum, a show with lunch, a shopping outlet or Atlantic City, and comes back by late afternoon. Most are open to residents 55, 60 or 65 and older, depending on the town, and cost anywhere from nothing for a local shopping run to more than $100 for a holiday show with lunch.

To find one, call your town's recreation department or senior center, or reach your county office on aging through the toll-free line, 1-877-222-3737. This guide explains how the trips work, what they cost, what to ask if your mom or dad uses a cane or walker, and how to check that a bus company is safe.

Who runs senior bus trips in New Jersey?

Most trips are run by town recreation departments, senior centers and senior citizens clubs. Each sets its own age rules, sign-up method and prices, so the first call is to your own town.

Here is how a few New Jersey towns describe their programs on their official websites. They show how much the rules vary.

TownWho can goHow it works
Morris Township, Morris CountyResidents 55+, plus guestsRegister with Parks and Recreation, 973-326-7371. Pay 30 days ahead. No refunds.
Berkeley Township, Ocean CountyResidents 65+Weekly Thursday trips. Call the trip line, 732-269-7077, after 4 p.m. on the listed date. No refunds.
Haddon Township, Camden CountyResidents 60+Day trips from Westmont Plaza. Reserve at 856-833-6247, pay by check.
Middletown, Monmouth CountyOpen to the public (21+ for Atlantic City)Coach trips from the senior center. Call 732-615-2265. Members pay less.

Morris Township runs its trips with the township Senior Citizens Club. In Berkeley Township you leave your name, registration card number and bus stop when you call.

If your town has no program, ask a neighboring town whether non-residents may join, or check with senior clubs that meet in churches and community halls. Our county guides list senior centers near you: Bergen, Essex, Monmouth, Ocean, Camden, or any county from the county guides.

Where do senior trips usually go?

Expect a mix of museums, shows with lunch, shopping, the shore and casinos. Holiday shows are among the most popular, and seats go fast.

Berkeley Township's published schedule for the first half of 2026 gives a good picture. It included the Naval Air Station Wildwood Aviation Museum, Liberty Science Center, Ellis Island by ferry, a guided painting class, Turtle Back Zoo, the Columbus flea market, Historic Smithville, Delicious Orchards, Lambertville antiques, Point Pleasant Boardwalk, Cape May and several Atlantic City days, with luncheons on the calendar too.

Middletown's senior center, for example, runs a holiday trip to a Christmas show with lunch at the Hunterdon Hills Playhouse, and it filled up well ahead of time. Evesham Township warns that spots on its trips fill quickly too. If your parent would enjoy a holiday show, sign up as soon as the flyer comes out. Our guides to holiday events for older adults and theater matinees have more ideas.

Casino trips are a category of their own. Evesham Township's 2026 casino trips, for example, included round-trip motor coach travel and $20 in bonus slot play, leaving from the Gibson House Community Center at 9 a.m. and returning in the early evening.

What do senior bus trips cost, and what is included?

Prices vary widely. Local shopping runs are often free. Trips with a show and a meal can run well over $100. Always ask what the price covers.

Two examples from 2026 town listings:

  • Middletown's holiday show and lunch at the Hunterdon Hills Playhouse cost $125 for members and $135 for non-members.
  • On several Berkeley Township trips, admission was paid separately. The Liberty Science Center trip listed $33 admission, Turtle Back Zoo $19, and the Ellis Island ferry $22 per person. A painting class was $27.99, cash only.

Before you pay, ask:

  • Does the price include admission, the meal, the tip for the driver and any guide?
  • Is lunch a set meal, or will your parent need money to buy food?
  • What is the refund policy if your parent gets sick? Many town programs give no refunds once you pay.
  • Can a friend or spouse who lives in another town come along?

Pay the way the program asks, usually a check made out to the township or the club, mailed or dropped off at town hall or the recreation office. Be wary of anyone who calls your parent offering a trip and wants payment by gift card, wire or cash app. Our guide to scams aimed at older adults explains the warning signs.

The best trip is the one where your parent already knows two people on the bus.

Can my mom go on a bus trip if she uses a walker?

Often yes, but ask before you sign up. Some programs require riders to be independent or to bring an aide, and the destination may involve more walking than the bus ride.

Programs set their own rules. Scotch Plains, for instance, says riders on its township senior bus must be self-reliant or accompanied by an aide. Middletown's senior center describes its membership as for independent residents 60 and older. If your parent needs help, a family member or paid companion can often ride along for the regular fare. Ask.

Questions to ask the trip coordinator:

  • Is the bus a coach with steps, or does it have a wheelchair lift? Can a walker or folding wheelchair go underneath?
  • Is there a restroom on the bus, and how often does it stop?
  • How far is the walk from where the bus parks to the entrance, the seats and the restaurant?
  • Are there stairs or hills at the destination? Is seating assigned?
  • Can my parent sit near the front, close to the door and the driver?
  • What happens if my parent feels unwell during the day? Who is the trip leader, and how do I reach them?

Federal rules say interstate charter bus companies that use motorcoaches must provide accessible service, with buses equipped with wheelchair lifts and securement areas. Ask the trip leader to request a lift-equipped bus early, before the trip fills. If a destination is a poor fit, a family drive may be easier. See scenic drives for a parent who can't walk far and our easy day trips with walking notes.

How can I tell if a bus company is safe?

Ask the trip organizer which bus company they use, then look up its safety record with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA). It takes a few minutes.

FMCSA, the federal agency that oversees bus companies, says an interstate for-hire motorcoach company generally must:

  • Have a USDOT number and operating authority from FMCSA.
  • Carry at least $5 million in insurance.
  • Provide accessible service under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

FMCSA rates companies Satisfactory, Conditional or Unsatisfactory. Satisfactory is best. A company with an Unsatisfactory rating should not be operating at all. Drivers must hold a commercial driver's license with a passenger endorsement and a valid medical examiner's certificate, and an interstate bus driver may not drive more than 10 hours in a row. You can research bus companies through FMCSA's Look Before You Book page.

On the bus, FMCSA suggests learning where the emergency exits and safety equipment are before the trip starts, and buckling up whenever the bus is moving.

How do I help a parent get ready for the first trip?

Sign up together, pick a trip with a short ride and an easy destination, and make sure the trip leader has your phone number. A first trip with a friend goes better than a first trip alone.

  1. Start small. A half-day shopping trip or a lunch outing is a gentler first try than a 12-hour day.
  2. Go with someone. A neighbor, a friend from the senior center or you. If your parent is new to the center, our guide to a first visit to a senior center can help.
  3. Write it down. Departure time, bus stop, trip leader's name, return time and what to bring, on one card in your parent's wallet.
  4. Pack light. Medications for the whole day plus a few extra hours, a photo ID, insurance cards, a snack, water, a sweater for the bus air conditioning, and a little cash.
  5. Share emergency information. Give the trip leader your number and a short list of medical conditions. Our printable emergency info sheet works well.
  6. Plan the ride home. Buses can run late in traffic. Make sure someone can pick your parent up at the lot, or that their car is parked in a well-lit spot.

A trip on the calendar gives your parent a reason to get dressed and out the door, and a chance to see familiar faces. For more ways to keep a social calendar, see staying connected in New Jersey. If your parent prefers to travel on their own schedule, NJ Transit reduced fares start at age 62.

faq.q: How do I find senior bus trips near me in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call your town's recreation department or senior center first. Many towns post trip flyers on their websites. The toll-free aging and disability line, 1-877-222-3737, can also connect you to your county office on aging.

faq.q: How do I sign my mom up for a senior bus trip?
faq.a: Call the program to ask how registration works, since each town is different. Some take reservations by phone on a set date, and most want a check made out to the township or club. Ask about the refund policy and what the price includes before you pay.

faq.q: Can my dad go on a senior bus trip if he uses a walker?
faq.a: Often yes, but ask first. Some programs require riders to be independent or bring an aide. Ask whether the bus has a lift or steps, where a walker can be stored, and how far the walk is at the destination.

faq.q: How much do senior bus trips cost in NJ?
faq.a: Local shopping runs are often free. Museum and shopping trips may cost little beyond admission, which is sometimes paid separately. A 2026 holiday show and lunch from one Monmouth County senior center cost $125 for members.

faq.q: Can non-residents go on another town's senior trips?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some towns limit trips to residents, while others welcome guests or the public. Call the program and ask.

faq.q: How do I check if a charter bus company is safe?
faq.a: Ask the organizer for the company name, then research its safety record through FMCSA's Look Before You Book resources. A company should have a USDOT number, operating authority and at least $5 million in insurance.
